stimuli.title: The Empty Plot
stimuli.body: Every afternoon, Lena walked past an empty lot between the bakery and the apartment building. Weeds pushed through cracked soil, and wind-blown wrappers gathered along the fence. Most people hurried by without looking.One Saturday, Lena carried a small cardboard sign to the lot. It read: FUTURE COMMUNITY GARDEN. Her neighbor Mr. Ortiz laughed kindly. "A sign cannot grow tomatoes," he said."No," Lena replied, "but it can grow an idea."At first, only Lena pulled weeds. The next morning, Mr. Ortiz arrived with a rake. By noon, the baker had brought a bucket of water. A week later, three families were turning the soil and building narrow garden beds from old boards.The work was slow. A late frost damaged the first seedlings, and rabbits discovered the lettuce. Still, the neighbors replanted. By midsummer, sunflowers leaned over the fence, beans climbed strings, and children counted red tomatoes.On the day of the first harvest, Mr. Ortiz handed Lena a tomato. "You were right," he said. "The sign grew more than an idea." Lena looked around at the neighbors sharing baskets and stories. The empty plot had become a place where people stopped instead of hurried.

stimuli.title: Fire on the Prairie
stimuli.body: A wildfire can destroy homes and threaten lives, but not every grassland fire is harmful. For thousands of years, lightning and carefully managed fires have helped maintain prairies.Prairie grasses store much of their living tissue below ground in thick roots. When fire moves quickly across the surface, the roots often survive. Within weeks, new green shoots appear. Many young trees, however, cannot survive repeated fires. Without occasional fire, trees and shrubs may spread until a prairie gradually becomes woodland.Fire also returns nutrients to the soil. Dead stems and leaves are changed into ash, which contains minerals plants can use. The blackened ground absorbs sunlight and warms quickly in spring. Some seeds even sprout more successfully after heat or smoke has affected them.Today, trained land managers sometimes conduct prescribed burns. Before lighting a fire, they study weather conditions, prepare firebreaks, and position crews with water and tools. A prescribed burn is planned for a specific area and time. If winds are too strong or the air is too dry, the burn is postponed.Fire is therefore both powerful and complicated. In the wrong place or under dangerous conditions, it can be disastrous. Used carefully in fire-adapted ecosystems, it can help preserve the prairie.

stimuli.title: Night Train
stimuli.body: The train writes silver lines through rain,then drums across the bridge.The sleeping farms are folded darkbeneath the moonlit ridge.Inside, a child leans on the glassand watches towns appear -a porch light, then a water tower,then nothing drawing near.The whistle sends a lonely noteacross the fields of wheat.The child counts every distant starwhile wheels repeat, repeat.

stimuli.title: Make a Rain Gauge
stimuli.body: You can measure rainfall with a clear plastic bottle, a ruler, small stones, tape, and scissors. Ask an adult to cut off the top third of the bottle. Place a layer of stones in the bottom so the bottle will not tip over. Pour in enough water to cover the stones.Use a ruler to mark a zero line at the top of the water. Then mark centimeters upward along the side of the bottle. Turn the cut-off top upside down and place it inside the bottle like a funnel. Tape the sharp edge.Set the gauge outdoors in an open area, away from trees and roofs. After rain, read the water level from the zero line, not from the bottom of the bottle. Record the amount, empty extra water until it returns to zero, and place the gauge outside again.

stimuli.title: The Mapmaker's Mistake
stimuli.body: In 1846, fourteen-year-old Eli worked in his uncle's print shop. One morning, a merchant ordered fifty maps showing a new road to the river port. Eli carefully copied the route onto a metal plate. He was proud when the first map rolled from the press.Then he noticed a problem. At a fork in the road, he had drawn the river route bending east instead of west. Travelers following the map could end up miles from the port. Eli's uncle was meeting a customer across town, and the merchant expected the maps that afternoon.Eli considered hiding the mistake beneath a thick ink mark. Instead, he stopped the press. He melted a small patch of wax onto the plate, recut the correct line, and printed a test sheet. The repair was not perfect, but the route was accurate.When his uncle returned, Eli showed him the spoiled maps and explained what had happened. His uncle studied the corrected sheet. "Paper can be replaced," he said. "Trust is harder to print twice."The merchant received the maps one day late. Years afterward, when Eli opened his own shop, the merchant became one of his first customers.

stimuli.title: Bats at Work
stimuli.body: Bats are sometimes described as frightening, but they perform valuable jobs in many ecosystems. Most bat species eat insects, fruit, or nectar rather than blood.An insect-eating bat can capture hundreds of insects in a single hour. By feeding on moths and beetles, bats may reduce the number of pests that damage crops. Fruit-eating bats spread seeds when they carry fruit or release seeds in new places. Nectar-feeding bats pollinate flowers as pollen sticks to their fur.Bats also help scientists understand environmental change. Because many bats live a long time and depend on healthy habitats, sudden declines in bat populations can warn researchers that an ecosystem is under stress.Unfortunately, bats face threats from habitat loss, pesticides, wind turbines, and disease. People can help by protecting caves, leaving dead trees standing when safe, reducing pesticide use, and installing bat houses in suitable locations.

stimuli.title: Books for Everyone
stimuli.body: Early American libraries were often private collections owned by wealthy individuals, churches, or colleges. In 1731, Benjamin Franklin and a group of craftspeople in Philadelphia created the Library Company. Members paid fees that were used to purchase books, and members could borrow from the shared collection.Subscription libraries spread, but they were not free. During the 1800s, reformers argued that communities should support libraries open to all residents. Towns began using tax money to establish public libraries. These libraries offered books, newspapers, lectures, and quiet places to study.Between 1883 and 1929, businessman Andrew Carnegie helped fund the construction of more than 1,600 public library buildings in the United States. Communities usually had to provide the land and promise to pay for staff and maintenance. This requirement was meant to ensure that each town would continue supporting its library.Modern public libraries still lend books, but many also provide computers, internet access, classes, meeting rooms, and digital materials. Their services have changed, yet their central goal remains: giving community members access to information.

stimuli.title: Two Views on the School Garden
stimuli.body: PASSAGE A: A Garden Worth GrowingOur school should turn the unused courtyard into a vegetable garden. Students could measure plant growth in science, calculate garden areas in math, and write observations in language arts. Working in teams would also teach responsibility. The harvest could be donated to a local food pantry. Although the garden would require work, it would turn an empty space into an outdoor classroom.PASSAGE B: Start SmallerA school garden sounds useful, but the courtyard project may be too large for the first year. Gardens need watering during weekends and summer, and tools, soil, and fencing cost money. Instead, each class could begin with two raised boxes near the building. After learning what works, the school could expand. A small successful garden would be better than a large garden that is neglected.
